subject: art-and-design
topicName: The Creative Process From Brief to Outcome

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The creative process is not linear — you move between research, experimentation, development and reflection in cycles.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Starting points can come from anywhere: a theme, an object, a technique, an artist, a memory, a place — but you must DEVELOP from them, not just illustrate them.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Your sketchbook is the EVIDENCE of your creative journey — it should show your thinking, experiments, decisions and reflections, not just finished pieces.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Critical reflection and evaluation are essential — they show you understand your own creative process and can make informed decisions.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Create a series of experimental studies exploring the creative process from brief to outcome. Annotate your process. | Research an artist or designer who works with the creative process from brief to outcome. Write a critical analysis of their approach and explain how it has informed your own work. | Evaluate the effectiveness of your experiments with the creative process from brief to outcome. Which approaches were most successful and why?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: A range of experimental studies showing different approaches to the creative process from brief to outcome, each annotated with media, technique and purpose. Show development from initial experiments  | A critical analysis naming a specific artist/designer, using specialist vocabulary, explaining their context and approach, and making clear connections to personal work. | A reflective evaluation identifying successful and less successful experiments, explaining WHY using technical and conceptual language, and showing how evaluation led to further refinement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Address ALL four Assessment Objectives — AO1 (develop), AO2 (refine), AO3 (record), AO4 (present) Show the FULL creative journey — from initial research to final outcome Annotate your work using specialist vocabulary (not just "I like it") Draw from primary sources wherever possible — real objects, not photos Experiment with a RANGE of media and techniques before selecting Make clear connections between artist research and your own developing work
